outputs.L1:
My grandmother places her feet in the sink of the bathroom at Sears to wash them in the ritual ablution for prayer—wudu—because she must pray in the store or else miss the mandatory prayer time for Muslims. She performs this with great poise, steadying herself with one plump, matronly arm braced against the automated hot-air hand dryer, having first removed her support knee-highs and set them aside, folded in thirds, and having handed me her purse and her packages to hold so that she may accomplish this august ritual and return to the ritual of shopping for housewares.

Respectable Sears matrons shake their heads and frown as they observe what my grandmother is doing—an affront to American porcelain, a contamination of American Standards by something foreign and unhygienic, requiring civic action and the possible deployment of disinfectant spray. They fluster about and flutter their hands, and I can see a clash of civilizations brewing in the Sears bathroom.

My grandmother, though she speaks no English, apprehends their meaning, and her reflection in the mirror seems to declare: I have washed my feet over Iznik tile in Istanbul with water drawn from the world's most ancient irrigation systems. I have washed my feet in the bathhouses of Damascus, over painted bowls imported from China, among the finest families of Aleppo. And if you Americans knew anything at all about civilization and cleanliness, you would build your washbasins wider in the first place.

She manages this with remarkable dignity, steadying her ample, motherly figure by pressing one arm against the automatic hot-air hand dryer. Beforehand, she has peeled off her support knee-highs, folded them neatly into thirds, and set them down, then handed me her handbag and shopping bags to carry so that she can complete this solemn rite and return to the ordinary rite of browsing for household goods.

The dignified Sears matrons scowl and shake their heads when they spot what she's doing—an insult to American porcelain, a defilement of American Standards by something alien and unclean, the sort of thing that demands intervention and perhaps a spritz of disinfectant. They fidget and wave their hands nervously, and I sense a clash of civilizations gathering steam in that Sears restroom. My grandmother understands exactly what they mean, even without a word of English between them, and the expression she wears in the mirror declares: I have cleansed my feet upon Iznik tile in Istanbul, using water drawn from irrigation systems as old as the world. I have cleansed my feet in the bathhouses of Damascus, over painted basins brought all the way from China, surrounded by Aleppo's finest families. And if you Americans understood the first thing about cleanliness or civilization, you would build your washbasins bigger to begin with.

In the middle of a Sears department store, my grandmother lifts her foot into the bathroom sink to perform wudu, the ritual cleansing that must precede Muslim prayer. The mandatory prayer time has arrived, and for her, missing it is simply not an option. And so, with the quiet certainty of someone who has done this countless times before, she turns to the only available source of running water and begins.

There is nothing hurried or ashamed in her movements. She carries out the ritual with dignity and poise, preparing herself methodically for the task. She removes her knee-highs and hands me her belongings to hold, entrusting me with the small ceremony of her devotion. Every gesture is deliberate, unbothered by the setting, guided by a lifetime of practice.

The other women in the restroom do not share her composure. They watch with expressions of disapproval and disgust, exchanging glances that need no translation. To them, the sight of a woman washing her feet in a public sink is unhygienic, improper—a foreign contamination of the standards they expect in an American bathroom. Their discomfort fills the small tiled space, thick and unmistakable.

Watching it unfold, I cannot help but see the moment as something larger than itself: a "clash of civilizations" playing out in miniature, right here between the sinks and the paper towel dispensers. Two ways of understanding the body, cleanliness, and the sacred have collided in the most ordinary of places, and neither side is willing to yield its sense of what is right.

My grandmother does not speak English, but she does not need the language to understand what is being said about her. She feels their judgment plainly, and she meets it with an inner conviction that never reaches her face. In her mind, she answers them—not with anger, but with the quiet pride of someone who knows exactly where she comes from. She has washed her feet in the great historic sites of the Muslim world, in mosques and holy places stretching back through centuries of tradition. Behind this simple act lies a heritage far older and more sophisticated than the strangers around her could imagine. Let them stare, she seems to say. They do not know what they are looking at.

# Ablutions at Sears

My grandmother washed her feet in the sink at Sears.

I remember standing beside her, a child made suddenly aware of the space my family occupied in the world. We had come for something ordinary—a set of towels, perhaps, or shoes for the coming school year—and the fluorescent aisles stretched around us in their American abundance. But when the hour of prayer arrived, my grandmother did not hesitate. She made her way to the ladies' restroom, and there, before the long row of porcelain sinks, she began her wudu.

She rolled her sleeves past her elbows. She cupped water in her weathered hands and drew it up her forearms, across her face, behind her ears. And then, balancing with a grace that belied her years, she lifted one foot and then the other into the basin, letting the cool water run between her toes as it had run for a thousand years before her.

The American women noticed.

I saw the way their faces shifted—the tightening of the lips, the exchanged glances, the barely concealed alarm. A matron in a floral dress stopped mid-motion at the mirror and stared, her expression curdling into something between disgust and disbelief. To these women, my grandmother was performing an act of trespass. A foot in the sink where hands were meant to go. A body ritual made public. Something unclean, something foreign, something that did not belong in the bright and orderly world of their department store.

They did not understand.

My grandmother spoke no English. Not a word. She could not have explained herself even had she wished to, and I do not think she wished to. She met their stares with a serenity that needed no translation. For she carried within her a lineage of cleanliness far older than the plumbing that so impressed the women around her. She was washing as her mother had washed, and her mother before her, in the courtyards of Istanbul where marble fountains sang, in the tiled hammams of Damascus, in the ancient streets of Aleppo where water and worship had been woven together since before this country had a name.

While these women recoiled at the sight of a foot in a sink, they did not know that they stood in the presence of a civilization that had bathed and purified itself while much of Europe still feared water as a carrier of disease. They believed cleanliness to be their invention, their inheritance, their measure of the modern and the civilized. They did not know that my grandmother's people had made ritual purity the very architecture of daily life, had built cities around the flow of clean water, had considered the washing of the body a sacred obligation long before soap was fashionable in the West.

And so the two worlds met there, in the humming light of a Sears bathroom—the one bristling with judgment, the other calm in its ancient certainty.

My grandmother finished her ablutions. She dried her feet, lowered her skirts, and turned to leave, her chin lifted, her dignity wholly intact. She did not look at the women. She did not need to. She had washed herself clean not only for God but against the small and narrow gaze of those who mistook their discomfort for superiority.

I was too young then to understand what I had witnessed. I only knew that I felt the weight of their eyes and the strength of her indifference to them. It was years before I could name what passed between them: a collision of civilizations disguised as a moment of mild embarrassment, a quiet insistence that dignity does not require permission, and that the measure of a people cannot be taken by those who have never bothered to learn what they are truly seeing.

She washed her feet in the sink at Sears. And she was the cleanest soul in that entire store.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short creative nonfiction piece about a Muslim grandmother washing her feet for wudu in a Sears bathroom, and the reactions of other shoppers.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ablution at Sears

My grandmother did not believe in waiting until she got home.

When the afternoon prayer arrived, it arrived—unannounced by anything but the angle of light through the department store windows and the certainty she carried in her chest like a second heartbeat. So she found the restroom near the men's suiting section, past the mannequins in their frozen poses, and she prepared to meet her God between the paper towel dispenser and the row of sinks.

I was eight, and I was mortified.

She hitched up the hem of her cotton sari and balanced on one foot with the grace of a woman who had done this ten thousand times, in ten thousand imperfect places. Her brown foot rose to the white sink. Water ran over her ankle, between her toes, down into the drain that had never known such a purpose. She whispered the names of God under her breath, unbothered, unhurried.

A woman in a denim jacket stopped mid-step. Her cart's wheel squeaked and went silent.

I watched the woman's face perform its calculations. Confusion first—the raised foot, the sink, the arithmetic that would not resolve. Then something harder settling into the mouth. She looked at me, as if I might explain, or apologize, or make my grandmother into something smaller and more familiar.

I looked at the floor.

Another shopper simply steered around us, eyes fixed forward with the practiced blindness of someone deciding this was not happening. A teenager smirked into her phone. But there was also a woman—older, gray at the temples—who caught my grandmother's eye in the mirror and gave a small nod, the kind that passes between people who have both knelt before something invisible.

My grandmother saw none of them, or all of them, and cared about neither possibility. Her lips moved. Her hands cupped the water. She wiped it over her hair, behind her ears, along her forearms in the sequence that was older than this country, older than this store, older than the very idea of shame I was drowning in.

When she finished, she lowered her foot to the tile and turned to me, water still bright on her skin.

*"Beta,"* she said. *"Why do you look so worried?"*

I had no answer she would have understood. I did not yet know that she was teaching me the most difficult prayer of all: how to belong to yourself in a room full of strangers. How to bring the sacred into fluorescent light and refuse to be ashamed of it.

She dried her feet with a brown paper towel, slipped back into her sandals, and took my hand.

We went to find a quiet corner near the fitting rooms, where she would spread a scarf on the industrial carpet and bow toward a Mecca she carried inside her like a compass needle, always trembling toward home.

I am older now than she was then.

I have prayed in airport corners and stairwells, in parking lots and borrowed rooms. And every time I raise water to my skin in a place not built for it, I feel her beside me—one foot lifted, unhurried, entirely herself, teaching me still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a moment where an immigrant grandmother performs a religious ritual in an American public space, capturing the cultural tension in a single flowing paragraph.
counterfactuals.output: The old woman kneels on the cracked sidewalk outside the DMV, unfurling her prayer rug against the concrete while a line of people shuffles past, some slowing to stare, others deliberately averting their eyes as though her devotion were a private thing accidentally spilled into public view. Her granddaughter stands a few feet away, phone clutched too tight, caught in that familiar ache of loving someone and wishing, just for this moment, that she would be smaller, quieter, less visible against the flat American afternoon—and then feeling the shame of that wish curdle in her chest. The grandmother touches her forehead to the ground with the unhurried certainty of someone who has done this five times a day for sixty years, through wars and border crossings and the long silence of a country that does not know her name, and she does not hear the man muttering, does not see the security guard hovering uncertainly by the glass doors, does not register the traffic or the heat rising off the parking lot. There is only the direction she has always faced, carried across an ocean like a compass needle that refuses to forget true north, and when she finally rises, dusting the grit from her knees, she looks at her granddaughter with such uncomplicated peace that the girl understands, all at once, that the tension she feels is entirely her own inheritance to reconcile—two worlds pressing against each other inside a single body, one of them praying, one of them apologizing, both of them home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a personal essay opening about your grandmother doing wudu in a department store bathroom, contrasting her dignity with the disapproval of American onlookers.
counterfactuals.output:
The first time I understood that my grandmother was brave, we were in the women's restroom at a Macy's in suburban Ohio.

She had her foot in the sink.

I want you to picture this correctly, because everyone who wasn't there pictures it wrong. She was not flailing. She was not, as the woman by the paper towels seemed to believe, doing something unsanitary or strange or aggressive. She was balanced with one hand against the cool tile wall, her cotton sock and sensible shoe set neatly on the floor beneath her, running water over her right foot three times, then her left, in the specific and ancient order of ablution that her own grandmother had taught her in a courtyard six thousand miles away. She was preparing to pray. She was, in the middle of a shopping mall that smelled of pretzels and perfume samples, making herself clean before God.

I was eleven, and I was mortified.

I remember the two women more clearly than I remember my grandmother's face that day, which tells you something about where my loyalties briefly, shamefully lived. One of them had stopped washing her hands to stare. The other made a sound—not a word, just a sound, that little exhalation through the nose that Americans deploy like a scalpel, the sound that means *can you believe this.* They looked at each other. They looked at me, because I was clearly *with* her, this small brown woman folding water over her skin, murmuring in a language they had decided was the language of people who did not belong in their restroom, their state, their country.

And my grandmother—

My grandmother did not hurry. That is the thing I have carried for twenty years. She did not shrink or apologize or offer the anxious smile that I was already, at eleven, learning to keploy as a toll for taking up space. She finished washing her foot. She dried it with the modesty of someone who has never once considered that her devotion might be a spectacle. She set her foot back into her shoe. And then she turned to the two staring women and gave them a small, serene nod—not defiant, not pleading, simply the acknowledgment one dignified person offers another—and walked out to find a quiet corner of the mall to pray.

It took me years to understand what I had witnessed. At eleven, I only knew that I was embarrassed, and that my embarrassment felt like a betrayal, and that both of those things were true at once and would remain true for a long time.

What I know now is this: I had watched a woman refuse to be made small.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a vivid literary vignette about a "clash of civilizations" happening in an ordinary American store bathroom, told from a grandchild's perspective.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Water Closet Diplomacy

My grandmother has never trusted a public bathroom, and today the public bathroom has confirmed every suspicion she ever harbored across two continents and seventy-three years.

We stand in the fluorescent hum of the Target restroom, and Lola—my mother's mother, who crossed an ocean with three children and one suitcase—is staring at the toilet like it has personally insulted her ancestors.

"Where," she says, "is the tabo?"

I am eight years old. I do not know how to explain that America does not believe in the tabo, the little water dipper that lived beside every toilet of her childhood, that in this country we have decided paper alone is sufficient, that we have staked our entire hygienic philosophy on absorption rather than irrigation.

"They don't have those here, Lola."

She looks at me with the expression of a woman witnessing the fall of Rome.

"Then how do people get *clean*?" The word emerges wet with disgust, heavy with the weight of an entire civilization's plumbing wisdom. "Paper? Only paper? *Anak*, this is not clean. This is *spreading*."

An American woman washes her hands at the sink, pretending not to listen, and I feel the great tectonic plates grinding beneath the tile floor—two worlds, two theologies of the body, meeting here between the toilet and the automatic paper dispenser that Lola has already declared "stupid" because it gives you one sheet at a time like it doesn't trust you.

She has come prepared. From her purse—that bottomless purse, that ark of preparedness—she produces an empty water bottle she saved from the food court.

"Fill this," she commands, handing it to me.

And so I become an ambassador between empires. I fill the bottle at the sink while the American woman's eyebrows climb toward her hairline, and I understand, dimly, that I am learning something my textbooks will never teach: that clean is not one thing but many things, that home travels inside people in the shape of small necessary rituals, that my grandmother will not be colonized by dryness.

When she emerges from the stall, victorious, she washes her hands for a full two minutes.

"Now," she declares, "I am clean. The American way—" she shakes her head, drying her hands on her skirt because she does not trust the air blower either "—the American way, you just *pretend*."

We walk out past aisles of things she finds equally suspicious: the pre-cut fruit, the dogs in strollers, the milk that lasts a month. But she holds my hand, and in her grip is the whole unspoken transmission of a people who refuse to forget how they came clean, even here, even now, even between the toilet and the sink of a country that has never once offered them a tabo.

I am eight. I do not yet know that I will spend my whole life like this—translating, filling water bottles, standing in the doorway between the world that made her and the world that is making me.

But I fill the bottle.

I always fill the bottle.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person narrative in which a proud elderly woman who speaks no English silently defends her heritage against judgmental strangers while washing her feet in a public sink.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Washing

They think I do not see them.

I see everything. Fifty years of watching has taught me this—the sideways glance is louder than any shout. The mother pulls her child closer as if my bare feet carry disease. As if the water I cup in my palms is not the same water that fell from her tap this morning.

I balance my heel against the cold porcelain and let the stream run over my ankle. In the mirror, a woman in expensive shoes stops mid-step. Her mouth makes a small shape. Disgust. I know that shape in every language, though I speak none of hers.

Let her look.

These feet walked across a border when I was younger than she is now. These feet carried three children when there was no one to carry me. These feet knelt on prayer mats worn thin as paper, in kitchens that smelled of cardamom and smoke, on the graves of a husband and a daughter I buried with my own hands. What does she know of feet?

The water is a prayer. She does not understand this. To her I am only an old foreign woman making a mess in a place where messes are not permitted. She sees the scarf on my head and decides she knows my whole story. She has read it somewhere, my story, in a newspaper that never asked my name.

*Wash between the toes,* my mother told me, kneeling beside me in another country, in another century. *Cleanliness is half of faith.* Her hands were rougher than mine are now. Her voice I can still hear when the water runs.

A young man enters and I feel him hesitate. The air changes. I do not lift my eyes. I have learned that dignity is not in the returning of a stare—it is in the refusal to be made small by one. So I continue. My hands move without hurry. I will not perform shame for an audience that has already written my verdict.

Let them wait for their sinks.

I am not sorry.

The woman in the expensive shoes says something to her child, something sharp, and I catch one word—a word they use like a stone. I have been struck by it before. It does not bruise anymore. I have outlived every mouth that ever threw it. I have outlived armies. I have outlived my own grief, which was harder than any of them.

I dry my feet with the cloth I brought, because I came prepared, because I have always come prepared, because a woman like me is never given the luxury of assuming the world will make room for her.

I lower my foot to the floor. I straighten my back—slowly now, the years live in my spine—and I gather my things.

At the door, I turn.

I look at them fully, all of them, these strangers who thought I could not feel the weight of their eyes. I let them see my face. Not angry. Not ashamed. Only *here.* Only unbroken.

I say nothing. I have no words they would accept, and they have earned none of mine.

But my grandmother's blood is in my veins, and her mother's before her, all the way back to women who washed and prayed and endured in lands these people cannot find on a map. I carry all of them out the door with me.

They will forget me by lunch.

I have already forgotten them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
